sens: Causing pain or suffering
Suffering physically or morally
Being tormented, going through great distress
Experiencing sorrow or grief
G3600.detail: 1. In its original sense, the word denotes the action of causing pain: this is why it is mostly found in the passive or middle voice, where the one undergoing the action suffers. 2. It refers to intense suffering, which can be physical, as in Luke 16:24 where the rich man in hell cries, "I am in agony in this flame," or moral, as when Jesus' mother searches for him "with anguish" (Luke 2:48). 3. This word expresses deep distress, an inner torment: the disciples accompanying Paul to Miletus are "grieved" (Acts 20:38) at the thought of not seeing him again, and this sorrow twists them. 4. The word can also describe the pain of regret or remorse: the rich man suffers not only from the flames but from knowing that he wasted his life.
G3600.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ὀδύνη (odúnē), which means "pain" or "suffering." This root expresses an image of rupture or inner tearing. The word belongs to a family that describes the ills of the body and soul. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, verbs like חוּל (to be in labor) or דָּוֶה (to be weak, sick) express this same idea of physical and moral suffering.
G3600.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels or Acts. Luke, who loves to describe feelings and emotions, is the only one to use it. It is first found in Luke 2:48, where Mary and Joseph suffer anguish while searching for the child Jesus. Then, twice in Luke 16:24-25, in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, where the rich man "suffers greatly" in the fire of hell — an eternal and irredeemable suffering. Finally, in Acts 20:38, Paul's disciples are "grieved" at his farewell. In each case, the word paints a vivid and inner suffering that knots the heart and torments it.
G3600.portee: This verb highlights the reality of suffering in the Bible: it is recognized and named, neither hidden nor minimized. For the Christian, it reminds us that Jesus knows human suffering — even that of his loving parents. But above all, it invites us to take seriously Jesus' words about eternal judgment: the parable of the rich man and Lazarus does not use this word by chance, to show that one who turns away from God will suffer an endless distress. It is a call to repentance and a life of charity.

sens: Intense physical pain
Moral suffering, heartache
Inner torment, agitation of the soul
G3601.detail:
1. Physical pain: the word primarily denotes suffering of the body, an acute and piercing pain. It is the cry of one who suffers in their flesh.
2. Grief and sadness: but above all, the word expresses moral suffering, the weight of a burdened heart. Paul experiences a "continual grief" (Romans 9:2) because of the fate of his brothers in Israel: it is a deep, personal, intimate pain that gnaws at him.
3. Inner torment: it is also the painful agitation of the soul, the anxiety that torments. One who loves money "falls into many troubles" (1 Timothy 6:10): they bring upon themselves a life of suffering and trouble, not all at once, but repeatedly and incessantly.
G3601.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes rupture, breakage, tearing — hence the idea of something that tears, that wounds. In Hebrew, the Greek Bible often translates words meaning "mourning" or "bitterness" with this word, reflecting the realities of the human heart consumed by sadness.
G3601.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament according to the provided usages. Paul uses it in Romans 9:2 to express his own anguish over Israel's rejection of the Gospel: it is a personal, visceral pain that does not leave him. In 1 Timothy 6:10, he describes the spiritual and moral consequences of the disease of greed, which throws those who cultivate it into a succession of troubles. In both cases, the word denotes an internal, deep suffering, that of the heart rather than the body, even if it includes the latter.
G3601.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Christian life can include legitimate and just suffering. Paul's pain for his people reveals a loving heart, capable of intercession and sacrifice. Conversely, 1 Timothy 6:10 warns that certain life choices — particularly greed — bring only torment. The word invites us to evaluate our attachments in light of our true peace in Christ.

sens: action of weeping and complaining
noisy and manifest expression of grief
regret or repentance expressed with tears
G3602.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of weeping abundantly, often accompanied by cries and complaints — it is not a simple inner sadness, but a mourning that is expressed loudly. In Ramah, one hears "weeping and great lamentation" (Matthew 2:18): Rachel weeps for her slaughtered children, expressing her grief through cries and tears that can be heard from afar.
2. More broadly, it is the feeling of deep sorrow itself, the tearing regret. In 2 Corinthians 7:7, Paul mentions "your tears" — not a silent resistance, but the outpouring of sadness and repentance before God. It shows that one truly suffers, that one does not hold back.
G3602.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb odúromai (to weep, to lament), which evokes the image of cries uttered in grief — it is a vivid and expressive word. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew taḿrur (bitterness, bitter tears), showing that lamentation is not a vague complaint but an intense and bitter pain. It is a word from the family of expressions of mourning and regret.
G3602.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 2:18, it depicts the scene of the slaughtered children in Bethlehem: it is a collective lamentation, the expression of a devastating national and familial mourning. In 2 Corinthians 7:7, Paul uses it in a more spiritual sense: the lamentation of the Corinthian community expresses their sincere repentance and love for Paul. In both cases, it is a sincere, unfeigned feeling.
G3602.portee: For the Christian, lamentation teaches us that sadness and regret are legitimate in the face of pain, loss, or sin. It is not a lack of faith to weep or express one's grief: it is an authentic part of our humanity. But the Bible also places lamentation within a horizon of consolation and grace — Rachel does not want to be comforted, but the Gospel comes precisely to bring that consolation which the world cannot give.

sens: king of Judah in the genealogy of Jesus
G3604.detail: Uzziah is a king of Judah whose name appears in the genealogy of Jesus according to Matthew. He is presented as the son of King Joram and the father of King Jotham, thus fitting into the royal line descending from David.
G3604.origine: The Hebrew name עֻזִּיָּה (Ouziyyâ) means "The Lord is my strength." It is the same character as King Uzziah of the Old Testament, also known as Azariah in some biblical texts. The Greek form Ὀζίας reproduces the Hebrew name.
G3604.emploi: Uzziah appears twice in the Gospel of Matthew, only in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8-9). He is named as a link in the genealogical chain connecting David to Jesus Christ. These two mentions correspond exactly to the two generations mentioned: Uzziah as the son of Joram (Matthew 1:8) and as the father of Jotham (Matthew 1:9).

sens: To emit an odor, generally unpleasant
To be perceptible by the sense of smell
To give off a characteristic bad odor (decomposition)
G3605.detail:
1. The verb denotes the natural action of emitting an odor, especially a strong or repugnant one. It is the nose that "smells" what the body or object exhales. In John 11:39, Jesus is about to raise Lazarus from the dead, but Martha protests: after four days in the tomb, the body "smells" already — she perceives the foul odor of decomposition that has begun.
2. The word applies to what becomes perceptible by smell, whether it is pleasant or repugnant. It is the sensitive emission of a volatile substance.
3. In the biblical context, it often evokes the stench associated with death and decay — the antithesis of life and freshness. Martha thus expresses her disbelief in the miraculous plan of Jesus: how can one raise a corpse that is already decomposing?
G3605.origine: The Greek verb ὄζω comes from a root that imitates the olfactory phenomenon: to smell, to sniff, to exhale. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew בָּאַשׁ (ba'ash), which means "to stink, to smell bad" — the same verb used in Exodus 8:14 for the dead frogs that infected Egypt. It is a concrete word, related to immediate and unpleasant sensation.
G3605.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: John 11:39. It is precisely at the moment when Jesus commands to roll away the stone from Lazarus's tomb. Martha, the sister of the deceased, expresses her practical concern — the odor of decomposition — as an apparent obstacle to Jesus's role. This small realistic detail underscores the magnitude of the miracle that will follow: raising a dead person whose body has already begun its transformation. The word thus has no abstract or moral dimension; it describes a raw physical reality.
G3605.portee: This word reminds us that the resurrection of Lazarus is not an abstract doubt or a theoretical question: it is a body that smells bad, a dead man for four days, whom Jesus brings back to life. Martha's faith is tested by the harsh reality — and it is in the face of this reality that Jesus's power over death is manifested with brilliance. For the Christian reader, it is a call not to make distinctions between the "spiritual" and the physical: God acts on the real, even the rawest, the most unpleasant.

sens: from the place or source from which one comes
from the starting point
for this reason, consequently
that is why, that is for this
G3606.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of place or source: "from where I came out" in Matthew 12:44 literally means the house from which the unclean spirit had come — the starting point, the spatial origin.
2. By natural extension, the word can designate a previous moment or state from which one returns, always with the idea of reverse direction: one returns from where one came.
3. In a more abstract register, "from where" indicates the hidden cause or reason: "Consequently" in Hebrews 2:17 translates this passage from the spatial to the causal — one slides from "from this place" to "therefore" or "consequently".
4. The word then takes on a logical or explanatory sense: "that is why" or "that is also why" (Hebrews 7:25), where the reason or conclusion of a previous statement is introduced without explicit connection — it is the thread of reasoning that unites the ideas.
G3606.origine: The Greek word ὅθεν (hothen) comes from the root of ὅς (hos, "who, which") and the suffix -θεν which marks ablation or provenance, literally "from where". In Hebrew, parallel expressions like מִשָּׁם (misham, "from there") or מֵאַיִן (meayin, "from where") convey the same idea. The suffix -θεν naturally creates a nuance of movement from a reference point.
G3606.emploi: The word appears fifteen times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and Hebrews. In the first two senses (spatial or temporal), it is found in Matthew 12:44 and Luke 11:24 for "from where the unclean spirit had come out". But the major usage of ὅθεν is logical or causal: in the epistles, especially in Hebrews (2:17, 3:1, 7:25, 8:3, 9:18, 11:19), it introduces a conclusion or deduction — "therefore", "that is why". In Acts 26:19, Paul uses it to announce the consequences of his heavenly vision. This shift from the spatial to the logical is characteristic of Greek: the language of space serves to express reasoning.
G3606.portee: This word shows us how the Bible thinks: it does not separate reasoning from direction, cause from origin. When the epistle to the Hebrews says that Jesus "that is also why" he can save us, it marks that every truth about his person entails a consequence for our lives — nothing is detached. Understanding ὅθεν is learning to read the Bible as a chain of linked thoughts, where each "from where" invites us to follow the thread of divine reasoning.

sens: Fine fabric, usually linen
Piece of fabric attached at the corners, used to cover or contain something
In a vision, linen object descending from heaven
G3607.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes fine fabric, particularly quality linen, used in clothing and furnishings. This is the ancient meaning of the word, inherited from classical Greek.

2. Later, it applies to a larger piece of fabric, attached at the four corners, which can be used as a tablecloth or as a veil. It is a flat, rectangular object, practical to handle and transport.

3. In Peter's vision in Acts 10:11, a "great sheet" descends from heaven attached at the four corners. Peter sees this linen object filled with clean and unclean animals, symbolizing the abolition of the distinction between permitted and forbidden foods in the new covenant.
G3607.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root, related to the Hebrew אֵטוּן (toile, linen). This origin reveals the influence of the Eastern world on Greek: the word was borrowed to name a common textile object in the Mediterranean. It literally denotes a fine and worked fabric, suitable for various uses.
G3607.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts, during the same vision reported twice (Acts 10:11 and 11:5). Peter describes a "great sheet" attached at the four corners, descending from heaven. This singular object, transported from heaven to earth, becomes the central symbol of the revelation that Peter receives: that God's grace now extends to the Gentiles, who had been considered unclean. The visionary context gives the word a strong theological significance, far beyond its usual material meaning.
G3607.portee: This vision of the descending fabric transforms Peter's understanding of the acceptance of Gentiles into the Church. It teaches him that what was once forbidden by the Mosaic Law is now purified by God himself. For the believer, this sheet symbolizes the abolition of religious boundaries and the universality of Christ's redemptive love.

sens: A piece of fine cloth used to wrap a dead body
Funeral cloth used for burial according to Jewish custom
G3608.detail:
1. The word refers to a strip of fine linen cloth used to wrap the body of a deceased person. This is what Jesus' friends did at the time of his burial: they took his body and wrapped it in strips with spices, "as is the custom of burial among the Jews" (John 19:40). These strips were placed around the corpse, visible and tangible — Peter, then John saw them lying in the tomb (John 20:5-6).
2. By extension, the word applies to the entire funeral cloth used for this practice. After the resurrection, when the disciples discover the empty tomb, the linen strips remain visible but detached from the body, a sign that Jesus rose without simply getting up (John 20:5-7). The cloth that had covered his head also remains, "not with the strips, but folded in a place by itself" (John 20:7), a detail that emphasizes the extraordinary nature of the resurrection.
G3608.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning fine linen cloth. In Hebrew, the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) translates the Hebrew words סָדִין (sadine, "fine linen garment") and פִּשְׁתֶּה (pishtéa, "linen") with this term. It is a specialized word for quality, refined cloths suitable for high-ranking funeral rites.
G3608.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, only in the context of Jesus' burial in John and Luke. John 19:40 describes the burial according to Jewish customs. Luke 24:12 and John 20:5-7 describe the moment when the disciples discover the empty tomb and see the linen strips left on the ground, a detail that marks the absence of the body and anticipates the testimony of the resurrection. The word always designates the same object: these strips used to wrap the deceased body before its resurrection.
G3608.portee: This humble word roots the resurrection narrative in physical reality and known funeral practice. The empty linen strips become silent witnesses: they prove that the body has disappeared, not by theft — the strips would have been moved together — but by a unique event that left the cloth in place. It is an invitation to believe in the bodily resurrection, real and astonishing, that transcends natural laws.

sens: belonging to the house, the home, the proper domain
concerning the affairs, the goods of the house
of the same family, of the same blood
belonging to someone's family (figuratively)
G3609.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the word refers to what belongs to the house or home, as opposed to what comes from outside or from a stranger. It is the familiar and intimate space of the household.
2. It also applies to the affairs or goods of the house, everything that concerns it directly and personally.
3. When speaking of people, it designates members of the same family, blood relatives: "If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household" (1 Timothy 5:8).
4. Figuratively, it describes those who belong to a spiritual family or community: "you are fellow citizens with the saints, members of the household of God" (Ephesians 2:19), or "toward the brothers in the faith" (Galatians 6:10), where believers are the family of God.
G3609.origine: The word comes from the root oîkos (house). It literally describes what is "of the house." The image is that of the home as the center of family life, the place where loved ones live. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words like dôd (beloved, relative) and shéër (flesh, kinship), notably in Isaiah 58:7 to speak of "the people of your family."
G3609.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to describe a relationship of closeness or belonging. In 1 Timothy 5:8, it refers to family members in the natural sense, with the exhortation to care for them. In Ephesians 2:19, Paul uses it figuratively to show that believers are no longer strangers but belong to the "household of God." In Galatians 6:10, it metaphorically describes "the brothers in the faith," the spiritual family of believers. Each time, the idea is one of intimate closeness and mutual responsibility.
G3609.portee: This word reminds Christians that their faith creates a true family. Believers are no longer strangers before God, but they enter into his house, his family. This implies concrete responsibilities: first toward their own in the natural sense (1 Timothy 5:8), then toward the "household" of faith (Galatians 6:10). The word invites consideration of the Church as a true family, not a mere association, with the tenderness and devotion owed to loved ones.

sens: a person employed in the service of a house, a family
slave or servant attached to a master
one who is entirely dependent on the authority of a master
G3610.detail:
1. The household servant is primarily one who lives in a master's house to serve him: he is a member of the familia, the household, charged with daily tasks. Jesus speaks of this in Luke 16:13 when he mentions the servant who cannot serve two masters — it is a relationship of concrete and total dependence on the one who pays and commands.
2. This word often designates a slave or servant, someone who belongs to the house and who does not have his freedom. Cornelius in Acts 10:7 calls his servants to send them to fetch Peter: these are men at his exclusive service, who obey him immediately.
3. The central image is one of absolute dependence. In Romans 14:4, Paul reminds that a servant of a master can only be judged by that master — he belongs to him, and only his master has authority over him. This submission is also recalled in 1 Peter 2:18: servants must submit to their masters with fear and respect, even if those masters are difficult.
G3610.origine: The word comes from the root "oikéô" which means "to inhabit a house": an oiketès is literally one who inhabits the house to serve. That is why it specifically designates a servant attached to a household, distinct from a mere worker or traveling companion. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word "eved" (עֶבֶד), which means both servant and slave.
G3610.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to designate household servants or slaves of the house. Jesus uses it in Luke 16:13 to illustrate the impossibility of serving two masters: the relationship is exclusive and total. In Acts 10:7, it is the neutral term to describe Cornelius' servants. Paul uses it in Romans 14:4 to remind that each one depends on his master, not on the judgment of others. In 1 Peter 2:18, it is an ethical exhortation: Christian slaves must obey even harsh masters. The word always emphasizes the relationship of dependence and obedience inherent to the status.
G3610.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds of the reality of servitude and submission in the ancient world — a reality that the epistles address without explicitly condemning it, but framing it within love and dignity. It also helps to understand the image of spiritual servitude: being a servant of a divine master implies unwavering obedience and total dependence. It is a powerful image of what it means to be a disciple — to belong entirely to Christ.

sens: To occupy a place, to reside there permanently
To establish oneself with someone, to share life
To take place in something, to sit there permanently
To spiritually reside in someone or something
G3611.detail:
1. The primary, very concrete meaning: to dwell in a place is to live there, to reside there. In 1 Timothy 6:16, God dwells in unapproachable light: He resides there, occupying its heart absolutely.

2. To dwell with someone describes a shared life: in 1 Corinthians 7:12-13, an unbelieving husband who dwells with his believing wife shares his daily life, his home. This is married life.

3. To dwell in something means to establish oneself there permanently. In Romans 7:18, Paul says that good does not dwell in him, meaning it does not sit in him as in its dwelling. Sin, on the other hand, dwells in us (Romans 7:17, 7:20): it has taken root, it reigns.

4. Spiritually, when the Spirit of God dwells in us (Romans 8:9, 8:11; 1 Corinthians 3:16), it is not a visit: it is a stable, intimate presence that makes us His temple. The Spirit takes up residence in us, just as God once dwelled in the temple of Jerusalem.
G3611.origine: The word comes from the Greek οἶκος (oikos), which means "house." To dwell is to remain in a house, to make a place one's home. The root evokes the idea of permanence: one does not dwell in a place of passage; one raises a family there, roots one's life there. In Hebrew, the verb יָשַׁב (yashav, "to sit") often carries the idea of remaining, of establishing oneself: to dwell is primarily to find where to sit, one's place, one's rest.
G3611.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, almost always in Paul. It takes three main forms: first, the concrete sense of residing somewhere (1 Timothy 6:16, 1 Corinthians 7:12-13). Then, and especially, Paul uses it in a spiritual, metaphorical sense: sin dwells in us (Romans 7:17, 7:18, 7:20), meaning it has established its reign in us, exercising power over our actions. Finally, the Spirit of God dwells in us (Romans 8:9, 8:11, 1 Corinthians 3:16), which for Paul is the decisive mark of belonging to Christ: it is a personal and transforming presence, no longer an absence. This presence of the Spirit that dwells makes each believer a living temple.
G3611.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals two truths that change everything. First, the Spirit of God does not visit: He dwells. It is a promise of permanent intimacy and not intermittent absence. Second, to dwell in us means to be master, to direct, to shape what one inhabits. When the Spirit dwells in us, He can transform our hearts from within. That is why Paul insists: ask yourself if the Spirit of God truly dwells in you, for that is the sign that you belong to Christ.

sens: Dwelling, habitation
Place of detention, prison (by euphemism)
G3612.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a dwelling, a home where one lives. It comes from the verb "to dwell" and simply describes a place where one resides.
2. By euphemism — a discreet or indirect way of speaking about an unpleasant reality — the word is used to refer to a prison, a dungeon. Acts 12:7 is the only known example: Peter is chained in prison when an angel of the Lord wakes him and miraculously frees him. It is a softened way of naming a place of captivity and punishment.
G3612.origine: The word comes from the Greek root oikéô (to dwell, to reside). It is formed like a noun of action or place: an oikêma is literally "that which is inhabited" or "a dwelling." Ancient Greek authors, such as the historian Herodotus, had already taken the habit of using this courteous word in place of cruder terms to speak of certain unpleasant places, hence its use as a euphemism.
G3612.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:7, where it designates the prison in which Peter is held. It is a discreet, almost polite term to name the place of captivity where the disciple spends the night before his supernatural escape. The use of a euphemism here perhaps emphasizes the contrast between Peter's humble and chained condition and the glorious intervention of the angel: the prison is merely a temporary "dwelling," which divine power crosses effortlessly.
G3612.portee: This passage reminds us that even in imprisonment — a situation where everything seems lost — God remains active and present. The angel who comes to free Peter embodies the certainty that no place of captivity, no human obstacle, can hinder God's purpose or His deliverance. For the reader, it is a sign of hope in the face of persecution and tribulation.

sens: Habitation, place where one resides
Image of the body as the house of the soul or spirit
Assigned residence for a creature by God
G3613.detail:
1. A dwelling is a habitation, a place where one lives — whether it be a house, a tent, or any space where one resides. Paul uses this word to speak of our present body as a "tent" (2 Corinthians 5:2), a fragile and temporary image.
2. By extension, the dwelling can designate the place assigned to a creature as its own territory or place. The angels who left their "dwelling" (Jude 1:6) abandoned the position and role that God had entrusted to them.
3. The word takes on a spiritual significance: it designates not only a physical lodging but a heavenly or eternal dwelling — the "heavenly home" that Paul longs for in 2 Corinthians 5:2.
G3613.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb oikéô (to dwell) and from the family of oikos (house). It originally designates the one who dwells, then their habitation itself — the place where dwelling occurs. This family of words is very ancient in Greek and very frequent in the Bible to speak of dwelling, house, or place where one resides.
G3613.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, in two very different contexts. In 2 Corinthians 5:2, Paul uses it to describe our current body as a "tent" — a temporary and fragile dwelling — in contrast to the "heavenly home" he hopes to put on. In Jude 1:6, the same word designates the "dwelling" proper that the rebellious angels have abandoned, meaning the place and dignity that God had assigned to them. In both cases, the word emphasizes the idea of an assigned or appropriate habitation for a creature.
G3613.portee: This word helps the believer understand their present state: the body is merely a temporary dwelling, a tent that one can leave. It nourishes Christian hope by reminding us that a true heavenly dwelling awaits us with God. It also illustrates that every creature — angels and humans — has a place entrusted to them by God, and that renouncing or abandoning it has serious consequences.

sens: Built structure, place where one lives
Real estate, property, heritage
Family, household, group of inhabitants
Human body, earthly dwelling of the soul
G3614G.detail:
1. A house is primarily a physical building, a structure where people reside: it is the concrete place of shelter and domestic life. When the Magi "entered the house" in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:11), they were crossing the threshold of a real building where Jesus' family lived. Matthew 7:24-27 compares two men who build their house on rock or sand — the image of the building is so central that the parables rely directly on it.

2. The house also refers to property, real estate, the entirety of material goods: one sells their house (Acts 4:34), one inherits it. It is the family heritage, wealth anchored in a place. Mark 12:40 mentions those who "devour widows' houses," meaning their possessions, their resources.

3. By extension, a house also refers to those who inhabit it: the family, the household, the home as a group of connected people. Matthew 12:25 states that "every house divided against itself cannot stand" — here it speaks of the inhabitants and their harmony, not the building. John 4:53 reports that the royal official "believed, he and all his house": his entire family.

4. Figuratively and more subtly, Paul calls the body a "house" or "earthly dwelling" (2 Corinthians 5:1): it is the material envelope where the soul or spirit dwells, as a soul inhabits a temporary house before going to join God.
G3614G.origine: The word οἰκία comes from the root οἶκ- which denotes the house, the habitat. It is related to οἶκος (house in a broader sense, domain, property), but οἰκία focuses primarily on the dwelling building itself. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word frequently translates the Hebrew בַּיִת (bayith), which has the same meanings: physical house, family, or material goods. The root evokes the idea of dwelling, of remaining established in a place.
G3614G.emploi:
The word house appears 76 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (especially Matthew, Mark, Luke). It is used first in a very concrete and everyday sense: one enters a house (Matthew 2:11, Mark 1:29), one builds it or goes out of it (Matthew 24:17, Luke 15:8). Luke and Mark often relate it in narratives where Jesus goes to someone's house — that of Simon, a tax collector, a sinful woman — all opportunities for encounter and teaching.

In a broader sense, the house refers to the property or the goods one possesses: Acts 4:34 recounts the sale of houses by the early Christians. Mark 12:40 and parallels speak of those who devour widows' houses — a crime of appropriating others' goods.

The word also takes on a collective sense: the house as a household, the family with all its inhabitants. 1 Corinthians 16:15 mentions the house of Stephanas, his people. John 14:2 ("In my Father's house, there are many rooms") plays on the image of the vast divine edifice filled with rooms for believers.

Finally, Paul uses house in a figurative sense for the body: 2 Corinthians 5:1 speaks of our "earthly tent," our "dwelling" (house) that we will have to leave.
G3614G.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the house is the privileged place of spiritual life: it is at home, in the intimacy of the household, that the bonds of family and faith are formed. The Gospels show Jesus entering houses, healing, eating, speaking to those who welcome him — the house is never a neutral or merely private place, but a space where God acts. Understanding also that our body is a temporary house where the soul dwells (2 Corinthians 5:1) invites us not to become overly attached to it and to prepare for our eternity with God. It is finally an image of the Church, the great house of the heavenly Father.

sens: Building or place of habitation
Home, group of inhabitants of a house
Family, lineage
Human body as the dwelling of the soul
Goods, property, heritage
G3614H.detail:
1. A house is primarily a building where one lives, a concrete place of habitation. Matthew 12:25 speaks of a "house divided against itself" to express internal discord: the image of the house as a structure that collapses illustrates what becomes disunited.
2. The word also refers to the inhabitants themselves, those who live under the same roof. John 4:53 reports that the father "believed, he and all his house": it is the entire household, from the master to the servants, that shares the faith.
3. By extension, this means a family or lineage — not only the daily household, but the continuity of generations of the same blood or social status.
4. The New Testament also uses this word figuratively for the human body: in 2 Corinthians 5:1, Paul calls the body "our earthly house," like a tent that shelters the soul.
5. Finally, "house" can refer to goods and property, everything that makes up the family heritage — a less common sense in our usage, but present when talking about wealth.
G3614H.origine: The Greek word οἰκία comes from the root of the word οἶκος (house, dwelling). In Hebrew, it frequently translates בַּיִת, which literally means the house, the building, but also the family and goods. The Greek word has gradually specialized: while οἶκος retained a broader sense (domain, property, family as a whole), οἰκία first focused on the dwelling building itself, before also designating the inhabitants and the household.
G3614H.emploi: The word appears about 9 times in the provided passages, mainly in Matthew and Mark. It is used first in a literal sense: a physical house where one dwells. But very quickly the biblical text employs it in a figurative manner: a house "divided against itself" (Matthew 12:25, Mark 3:25) becomes the symbol of disunity and moral or spiritual collapse. The context of the appearances is often one of faith and welcome: believing in the word of Jesus means opening one's house and heart. The word can finally refer to the people of a house, its entire household (John 4:53: "all his house"), showing that the house is not just a building, but a unit of common life.
G3614H.portee: Understanding that a united house reflects divine order and is the foundation of faith transmitted: this is why Jesus invites to welcome his messengers "into one's home." Conversely, a divided house cannot stand — a powerful image of what happens when Christ is not at the center. For the believer, reflecting on the spiritual unity of one's own house is to take seriously the first place where faith must be demonstrated.

sens: the members of a household, the family and the servants living under the same roof
by extension, the close ones of someone
G3615.detail: 1. The word designates the people who belong to a house, who live together — family, servants, slaves. In Matthew 10:25, Jesus speaks of the "people of his house" in contrast to the "master of the house": these are all those who are not at the head of the household. 2. By extension, the word applies to all those who are closely related to someone, their loved ones. In Matthew 10:36, Jesus warns that a man "will have for enemies the people of his house" — those of his own family, his intimates.
G3615.origine: The word comes from oïkía, which means "house, dwelling." It literally designates what belongs to the house, what is a member of it. It is very close to the word oïkéios ("familiar, domestic"), of which it is somewhat a variant. This family of Greek words always refers to the idea of house and domestic life.
G3615.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, only in Matthew in chapter 10. In both passages, Jesus uses it to speak of the inhabitants of a house. First in Matthew 10:25, where he outlines the common fate of the disciple and the master: just as the master suffers insults (here, being called Beelzebul), the servants will suffer the same. Then in Matthew 10:36, where Jesus announces a painful division: following Jesus can create hostility even within the family — those with whom one shares the house can become adversaries. The usage emphasizes the possible rupture between blood ties and commitment to Jesus.
G3615.portee: These two verses remind the disciple that faithfulness to Jesus can come at a relational cost. The word "house" evokes intimacy, trust, the space where one feels safe — and it is precisely there that opposition can arise. It is a call not to fear family breakups when they are the price of discipleship, and to accept that following Jesus redefines relational priorities.

sens: Exert authority in one's home, ensure its governance and management
Administer domestic affairs responsibly
G3616.detail:
1. The verb describes one who assumes authority and management of a house, a family — which encompasses material organization (meals, maintenance), but also discipline and instruction of children. In 1 Timothy 5:14, Paul encourages young widows to remarry and to "manage their house," in other words, to take on this family responsibility rather than depend on outside help. It is an active, positive form of domestic governance.
2. The word implies intelligence and mastery: it is not just about living in a house, but taking care of it wisely. This includes daily decisions: education, budgeting, discipline. Paul uses this term to show that this activity is worthy and is a form of respectable work.
G3616.origine: The verb is formed from "oikos" (house, home) and "despotès" (master, lord): literally "to be the master of the house." The corresponding Hebrew word in the Old Testament would be close to "master of the house." The family of these words appears in the New Testament to designate those responsible for a household or a community.
G3616.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 5:14. Paul uses it in the context of young widows whom he urges to remarry and build a stable family life. By choosing this term, he values the role of homemaker as a serious and responsible vocation, and not as tyrannical domination. The context emphasizes autonomy and dignity: not being a burden, but capable of managing one's oikos.
G3616.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that managing a household, often seen as minor, is in reality a noble charge and requires vigilance, wisdom, and responsibility. For one who manages their household, it is an invitation to do so with intention and wisdom; it is also a term that values women in their roles as mothers and homemakers, far from devaluing them.

sens: One who owns and governs a house, a dwelling
One who commands servants and workers in his property
One who welcomes guests, who receives visitors
The house itself, the home
In a figurative sense: one who holds authority and spiritual wealth
G3617.detail:
1. The master of the house is primarily one who owns and governs a dwelling: it is the owner who is responsible for it. In Matthew 24:43, the master of the house must ensure that a thief does not "break into" his house — he is the vigilant guardian.

2. This master commands servants and workers. In Matthew 20:11, workers receive their wages from the master of the house; in Luke 14:21, the master sends his servant to accomplish a mission among the poor: he is a man of authority who organizes work.

3. The master of the house is one who receives, who welcomes: he opens his home to guests or visitors. This image of hospitality colors several passages where he invites or refuses to invite.

4. By extension, the word can designate the house itself, the home as a unit of habitation and domestic life.

5. Jesus uses the image of the master of the house to speak of one who possesses spiritual wealth: in Matthew 13:52, a "scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven" is like a master who brings out of his treasure "things new and old" — he is rich in divine knowledge and dispenses it wisely.
G3617.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: oïkos ("house," "dwelling") and despotês ("master," "lord"). It is thus literally the "master of the house." This composition reflects the social reality of the Greco-Roman and Jewish world: the house (oïkos) is a fundamental economic and social unit, directed by a head of family who is the despotês. The word is well attested in common Greek and in the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.
G3617.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the four Gospels, concentrated mainly in Matthew. It never appears in the rest of the New Testament. Jesus and the narrators use it to describe concrete situations of daily life: masters who oversee their property (Matthew 24:43, Luke 12:39), who command their servants (Luke 14:21), who pay workers (Matthew 20:1, 20:11). Jesus also uses it for parables and spiritual teachings: in Matthew 13:27 and 13:52, he uses the image of the master of the house to speak of one who understands the kingdom of heaven. The word is always linked to the idea of authority, responsibility, and management of a dwelling.
G3617.portee: The image of the master of the house illuminates several spiritual truths. It shows that vigilance is an essential virtue: one who possesses must watch over what is entrusted to him (Matthew 24:43). It also teaches that authority comes with duty towards others: the master must treat his servants well and provide for those who suffer (Luke 14:21). Finally, it invites the believer to be like the wise master of the house who knows how to draw from his spiritual treasure — his knowledge of God — the best to nourish others (Matthew 13:52). It is an image of responsible management and generosity.

sens: To construct a building, a physical structure
To rebuild or restore what has been destroyed
To strengthen, encourage, fortify someone in their faith or character
To establish, found something lasting
G3618.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to construct a house, a building. The wise man in Matthew 7:24 "builds his house on the rock," with walls and foundations. A landowner "builds larger barns" in Luke 12:18. Workers "build" towers and temples, like Solomon who "built a house" for the Lord in Acts 7:47.
2. The word can also mean to reconstruct: it is announced that the temple will be "rebuilt" in three days (Matthew 26:61). Adversaries say to Jesus, "rebuild" what has been destroyed (Matthew 27:40).
3. In a figurative sense, which is very common in Paul, "to edify" means to strengthen someone in their faith, love, or Christian character. One who speaks in tongues "edifies himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4), and it is by encouraging one another that we "build each other up" (1 Thessalonians 5:11). The Church is "built" spiritually in Acts 9:31.
4. To establish or found something fundamental: Jesus says, "on this rock I will build my Church" (Matthew 16:18), creating a community meant to last. Paul refuses to build "on a foreign foundation" (Romans 15:20), meaning to rely on the work of another apostle.
G3618.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "house" (oîkos) and "to build" (dém-, démo). It is the word used in the Septuagint (the Greek Bible) to translate the Hebrew בָּנָה (bânâh), which has exactly the same meaning of physical construction and then, figuratively, of formation or establishment. The family of the word includes terms like "master of the house" and "builder." This image of construction becomes, in the New Testament, a powerful symbol of spiritual formation.
G3618.emploi: The verb appears 38 times in the New Testament, notably in Matthew, Luke, and Paul. In the literal sense, it speaks of the construction of houses, barns, temples, and towers: it is the ordinary activity of men (Matthew 7:24-26, Luke 12:18, Acts 7:47). But the figurative sense predominates in Paul, who uses it to describe the spiritual and moral growth of the Church and Christians: in 1 Corinthians 8:1, 10:23, Paul reminds that "knowledge puffs up, but love builds up," emphasizing that every action should serve to strengthen the faith of others. This word also appears in the passive voice, describing how the Church builds itself up (Acts 9:31) or how each one is built as a living stone (1 Peter 2:5). Jesus uses the word metaphorically to say that he will build his Church (Matthew 16:18), giving the word an eschatological and foundational dimension.
G3618.portee: This word teaches the believer that spiritual life is not given all at once, but is "built" gradually, stone by stone, through listening to the Word, prayer, and mutual support. It also reminds that each person, through their words and actions, contributes to building up or weakening their brother in faith. Finally, the image of Jesus building his Church invites the Christian to see their role in this great project of God: to participate in the construction of the body of Christ.

sens: The act of building, erecting a building
The building itself, the physical construction
The spiritual progress of a person or a Christian community
The act of strengthening or reinforcing the faith of others
G3619.detail:
1. The act of building, erecting a building: the word primarily refers to the work of the builder who assembles stones and materials. Jesus, leaving the temple, says to his disciples: "See these buildings" (Matthew 24:1), pointing out the stones of the temple that Herod had erected.

2. The building itself, the physical construction: once the work is completed, the word refers to the result, the finished building. Mark mentions that all the disciples were looking at "these buildings" (Mark 13:1), admiring the stones of the temple.

3. The spiritual progress of a person or a Christian community: the Bible transposes the image of the building to the spiritual world. The apostles speak of "edification" to describe how believers grow, strengthen, and consolidate in faith. Paul writes: "Let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification" (Romans 14:19), inviting believers to support one another to grow together.

4. The act of strengthening or reinforcing the faith of others: taking care of someone else's spiritual growth. Paul says that one who prophesies "edifies" others (1 Corinthians 14:3), meaning he strengthens, encourages, and helps them progress in their Christian life.
G3619.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "oîkos" (the house) and "démo" (to build). It literally means "to build a house." The Hebrew word "banah" (to build), very common in the Greek Old Testament, is regularly translated by this term. It is a natural and concrete word, borrowed from the everyday vocabulary of construction to speak of spiritual growth.
G3619.emploi: In the New Testament, the word appears eighteen times, mainly in Paul and in the letters to the Ephesians. Jesus first uses it in a concrete sense when speaking of the temple (Matthew 24:1, Mark 13:1-2). But Paul takes it up and makes it the key word for spiritual development: he speaks of edification in the assemblies (1 Corinthians 14 speaks repeatedly of what builds up the assembly), of personal edification (2 Corinthians 12:19), and of the edification of the body of Christ which is the Church (Ephesians 4:12, 4:16). Edification thus becomes the goal of all spiritual gifts and ministries: everything that is said or done in the assembly should serve to strengthen the faith of those who listen.
G3619.portee: This word teaches us that the Christian life is a patient and collective construction. Every word, every kind act has an effect: that of strengthening those around us in their faith. This changes our perspective on church life: not seeking to shine or impress, but to solidify the community, to help each one better know Christ and root themselves in Him.

sens: To manage the goods and affairs of a house or estate as a responsible manager
In a broader sense, to direct, organize, and put in order any matter
G3621.detail:
1. The verb first describes the task of the manager or steward who oversees the goods of a master. It involves concrete management: taking account of income, monitoring expenses, maintaining the estate in good order. In Luke 16:2, the master asks his steward to "give an account of his administration" and to no longer manage his goods — it is clear that the word refers to the daily and responsible management of an estate.
2. More broadly, the verb extends to any act of organization or direction: to administer then means to arrange, regulate, put in order according to a thoughtful plan. This is the sense of the derived noun "economy" or "administration" when speaking of a divine or human organization or arrangement.
G3621.origine: The verb comes from the noun οἰκονόμος (oikonomos: the manager or steward), itself composed of οἶκος (house) and νέμω (to distribute, to share). The word paints the image of one who distributes and arranges the affairs of the house. In Hebrew, the idea is close to words meaning "to nourish" or "to provide" (like כּוּל), hence the link between managing an estate and ensuring its sustenance.
G3621.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 16:2, in the parable of the dishonest steward. Jesus uses the word to show how a master expects his servant to manage faithfully and account for his administration. The context emphasizes the responsibility of the manager before his master: he must be trustworthy and cannot embezzle. This passage reveals that "to administer" is not absolute power, but a service to be rendered according to the expectations of the one who entrusts the goods.
G3621.portee: This word teaches that all power or responsibility given by God is a deposit awaiting accountability. Like the steward in the parable, the believer is merely a manager of the goods and gifts received (time, talents, money, responsibilities): one day, he will have to account for them. Faithful administration is therefore not a matter of wealth, but of integrity and honor towards the one who entrusts us with his possessions.

sens: Function of a manager or steward responsible for managing the property of a master
Charge, mission, or responsibility entrusted to someone
Management, execution of a plan or design
Divine disposition or God's plan for the world and humanity
G3622.detail:
1. The primary meaning refers to the function and role of a steward who receives from the master the responsibility to manage his property and affairs. The clearest example is the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16:2-4), where the master asks the steward to "give an account of his administration": this is the concrete use of the word for the work of a servant or slave tasked with running a household.
2. The word then shifts to the meaning of charge or mission: Paul says he fulfills his charge "against his will" (1 Corinthians 9:17), speaking of the weight of his responsibility. It is a task that falls upon him, a duty to fulfill.
3. In a broader sense, it signifies the execution of a plan or overall management. Ephesians 1:10 speaks of putting a design into "execution": God executes His plan for the world.
4. Finally, in the Pauline epistles, the word takes on a profound theological meaning: it is the administration or dispensation of God's design, His plan of salvation for humanity (Ephesians 3:2, 3:9; Colossians 1:25). It is the way God organizes and distributes His grace to mankind.
G3622.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to manage a house" (literally: "law of the house"). It is a term borrowed from Greek domestic and economic life, then transposed to speak of any form of management or administration. In Isaiah 22, the Septuagint (Greek version of the Old Testament) uses this word to mean "function" or "government," showing how the Greeks understood the idea of responsibility and authority.
G3622.emploi: Paul uses this word nine times in the New Testament, almost always to speak of the role of minister or apostle. In 1 Corinthians 9:17, he uses it for his own mission: he must proclaim the Gospel, it is a charge entrusted to him. In Ephesians (1:10; 3:2; 3:9) and Colossians 1:25, the word rises to a theological level: it is God's grand plan itself, His administration of salvation and the unification of all things in Christ. Finally, in 1 Timothy 1:4, Paul speaks of teaching as falling under this kind of coherent plan. The word moves from the concrete (the management of a household in the literal sense) to the abstract (God's eternal design).
G3622.portee: This word reminds the Christian that every mission, every ministry, is a responsibility entrusted by God. Just as the steward must give an account to his master, the believer must answer for the charge given to him. More broadly, it invites us to see the history of salvation, grace, and the Gospel, not as random occurrences, but as a design organized and ordered by God. This gives meaning and confidence to those who serve.

sens: One who administers the property or house of another, generally a slave or a freedman
One who manages the finances or property of a person or community
One who distributes or organizes according to a plan
One who exercises a responsibility entrusted in the Church or before God
G3623.detail:
1. The steward is primarily a servant tasked by his master to manage the house or estates: he is a steward who oversees people, provisions, and daily administration (Luke 12:42: "the faithful and wise steward whom the master will set over his household"). He can be a slave or a freedman, but he receives a position of trust and limited authority.

2. In towns and cities, the steward becomes a magistrate who administers public finances: he is the treasurer responsible for the accounts (Romans 16:23: "Erastus, the city treasurer").

3. The word expands to designate one who manages the mysteries of God, distributing them to men as a steward distributes the entrusted goods (1 Corinthians 4:1: "the stewards of the mysteries of God"). The apostle is not the owner of the mystery; he is responsible for it.

4. More broadly, it refers to one who, in the Church, exercises a pastoral charge or spiritual responsibility as a servant of Christ (Titus 1:7). Every Christian is also an administrator of the gifts received from God (1 Peter 4:10: "each of you, as good stewards of the varied grace of God").
G3623.origine: The Greek word οἰκονόμος comes from the root οἶκος (house) and the verb νέμω (to distribute, to allocate, to manage). The steward is literally one who "manages the house" or "distributes the resources of the house." This foundational image—the steward responsible for another's property—structures all uses of the word, from the simple servant in the parables to the ministers of the Church. The Hebrew word עַל (upon, in charge of) which designates the responsible one or administrator, was often translated by this Greek term in ancient translations of the Old Testament.
G3623.emploi: The word appears about 10 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the teachings of Jesus and in Paul's epistles. In the parables of Luke (12:42 and 16:1–8), the steward is the central character illustrating the faithfulness expected of one who manages what does not belong to him. In 1 Corinthians 4:1–2, Paul applies the title of steward to himself and his colleagues to express that the apostles are merely responsible servants before God. In Titus 1:7 and 1 Peter 4:10, the term extends to pastors and Christians in general, emphasizing that every charge or gift in the Church is a stewardship entrusted. The meaning gradually shifts from concrete management to spiritual responsibility.
G3623.portee: This word reminds the believer that nothing truly belongs to him: all the gifts, talents, resources that we manage—our possessions, our time, our spiritual gifts, our ministry—are entrusted by God and we will be held accountable for them. The faithful steward in Jesus' parables illustrates that faithfulness in small things and wise use of what is entrusted to us are the true measures of a disciple. For the pastor as well as for every Christian, this image invites humility: we are not owners, but responsible stewards.

sens: Building or dwelling where a person or family lives
Group of inhabitants of a house: household, family
Descendants, lineage, or people ("house of Israel", "house of David")
Religious building: temple or sanctuary
The human body considered as a dwelling
Place where the Church gathers and is edified
G3624G.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: it is the building where people live, with its walls and roof. Jesus healed several inhabitants there, such as the paralytic who returned home (Matthew 9:6) or Peter's mother-in-law, in Mark 2:1.

2. "House" also refers to the people who inhabit it: the family, the household. When the jailer of Philippi and all his household convert, it is his entire "house" that joins the Church (Acts 11:13).

3. By extension, the word describes a lineage or an entire people: the "house of Israel" or the "house of David" means all the people descended from that founding father (Matthew 10:6, Luke 1:27).

4. A "house of prayer" is the temple, the building dedicated to divine worship (Matthew 21:13). The expression refers to the sanctuary where God dwells.

5. Jesus also compares the human body to a "house" inhabited: unclean spirits can come out of it and return (Matthew 12:44, Luke 11:24).

6. Peter calls Christians themselves a "spiritual house", built as a living temple where God dwells (1 Peter 2:5).
G3624G.origine: This word comes from ancient Greek and corresponds to the Hebrew "bayit". The basic notion is that of a dwelling or a construction. In Hebrew, the same word designates the physical house, the family, and the lineage—a semantic richness that Greek adopts. The idea of rooting, of a place where one dwells and from which one is born, unites all these meanings.
G3624G.emploi: The word appears about 73 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels, it mainly refers to the housing of individuals: Jesus heals there (Matthew 9:6, Mark 5:38), dines there (Luke 7:36), and teaches there (Mark 7:17). In Luke, "house" takes on a domestic hue: that of Mary and Martha, that of Zacharias. In Matthew, it becomes genealogical: "house of Israel" or "house of David". In Mark, it is an intimate, almost secret refuge, where the mystery of the Kingdom is revealed. In John, it is the temple or the heart of worship. In Acts, the first Christians gather "from house to house" to pray and break bread (Acts 2:46, 5:42). Paul adds the ecclesial image: the Church is the "house of God" (1 Timothy 3:15, Hebrews 3:2, 1 Peter 4:17).
G3624G.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the house is a holy place: it is where one receives Jesus, prays, and shares life. The Church itself is a "house" where everyone has a place, built on Christ who is the cornerstone. This image invites the believer to see their home and community as spaces of divine presence, healing, and brotherly communion.

sens: A building where one lives
The people who live together in a house, a family
The entirety of a person's descendants, a dynasty or a people
The temple of Jerusalem, dwelling of God
The Church, community of Christians
G3624H.detail:
1. The most common meaning: a building intended for habitation, a dwelling. It is the place where a person or family resides, where they live daily (Acts 18:8).

2. By extension, the house also refers to the inhabitants themselves, that is, the family or the group of people living together. When we say "all his house", we refer to all the family members (Acts 18:8: "Crispus, the chief of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his family").

3. The word is used to designate the descendants of a person, their entire lineage: the "house of Israel" is the whole people descended from that name, the "house of David" is his dynasty and descendants (Matthew 10:6: "go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel").

4. In the Old Testament, the temple is called the house of God, because it is the place where God resides among His people, His earthly dwelling.

5. In the spiritual sense, the Church is the house of God: it is no longer stones that make the house, but the Christians themselves, living stones (1 Timothy 3:15: "how one ought to conduct himself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God").
G3624H.origine: The Greek word οἶκος comes from a very ancient root that evokes the idea of dwelling and habitat. In Hebrew, it corresponds to בַּיִת (bayit), which means house, and it designates both the physical building and the family and lineage. The same Greek root has given rise to words like "economy" (management of the house) or "ecology" (study of the house-earth). The word has gradually enriched itself: from the physical house, it took on the meaning of family, then of an entire lineage, and finally of a spiritual dwelling.
G3624H.emploi: The word οἶκος appears 32 times in the New Testament. It is first used in the literal sense: a concrete dwelling where people live (Acts 18:8). Very often, it refers to the family or the household, that is, all the inhabitants together (Acts 7:10: Joseph "was made governor over Egypt and all his house"). The New Testament also uses it to speak of the entire lineage of a person: the house of Israel (Matthew 10:6), the house of David (Luke 1:27; 2:4). For the temple, the house of God refers to its function as a divine dwelling. Finally, in the writings of Peter and Paul, the Church is described as the house of God or the spiritual house of the Lord (1 Timothy 3:15; Hebrews 3:2-6; 1 Peter 4:17), an image that shows that the believers themselves constitute this living house.
G3624H.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the Church is not primarily an organization, but a family, a house where people know each other and help one another. Understanding that the Church is the house of God helps to see that the relationship among believers should not be cold or distant, but familial and intimate. It is also a call to respect the house of God, whether in its physical body or in its local community.
